messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 37-year-old financial analyst, divorced for the past three years. The year before his marriage ended, he was abducted from his car after a late evening at the office and held captive for twelve days in a windowless basement. The men who took him were never identified; the case remains open, gathering dust in a precinct file cabinet. During those days, he was kept in near-total silence for hours at a stretch — the kind of quiet that pressed against his ears and made his own breathing sound like a betrayal. Occasionally he heard children crying from somewhere else in the house, thin and frightened. Once, one of the captors placed a hand flat on his shoulder, a gesture of reassurance that felt more terrifying than the threats.

Two years after his release, David still cannot shake the smell of that basement — mildew, sweat, the metallic tang of his own fear. The memory often arrives with a clarity that feels more real than his actual present: he can almost feel the rope around his wrists, the cold concrete floor. When it happens, he is overcome with the conviction that he acted in ways that go against who he is. He had cooperated, had not fought back, had answered their questions. The shame of that compliance sits in his chest like a stone. And because the men who did this to him have faced no consequences, the feeling that he is still an object — something to be used, then discarded — never fully leaves him.

That feeling feeds on the smallest cues. At home, a sudden silence — the refrigerator compressor shutting off, the furnace clicking quiet — sends his heart racing and his body bracing. He has become hypervigilant even inside his own locked apartment, scanning doorways and windows, struggling to fall asleep because staying alert feels like a matter of survival. Living at that pitch of constant alertness, he found ordinary sounds had become laden with warning — the creak of a floorboard read as a footstep, the distant murmur of a neighbor's television as muffled voices — and each one confirmed what his body already knew: that danger was never far. The constant watchfulness makes his mind loop back to the basement: the more on guard he is, the more vividly the memories return, each one dragging the next. And each memory reinforces his sense of having been reduced to a thing.

He now avoids physical affection entirely. A colleague’s hand on his shoulder at a meeting makes him stiffen; his ex-wife’s hug in the months after the abduction felt like a trap. He cannot bear to be near children crying, so he crosses streets, leaves stores, has told friends he can’t be around their kids. Even at his cubicle in the financial firm, the quiet hush of the office after hours — when the last analyst leaves and the ventilation hum drops away — triggers the same electric dread. That dread, in turn, resurrects the feeling of being a dehumanized hostage. The more he feels like an object, the more hyperattentive he becomes to the exact kinds of sounds that once signaled his helplessness: silence, crying, the approach of footsteps.

Relationships became impossible. His ex-wife could not understand why he flinched from her touch or why he insisted on sleeping with the television on. She left him two years ago, and since then he has lived alone, his apartment a fortress of white-noise machines and talk radio. At work, he is competent but distant; his colleagues think he is simply reserved. The reality is that he cannot afford to lower his guard.

What finally brought him to seek help was a bad week. A child wept in the grocery aisle, and he abandoned his cart and walked out. That night, the memory came so clearly he smelled the basement again and believed for a moment he was still there. He only calls himself a survivor when he thinks of the legal case; inside, he believes he is still waiting for something — justice, or perhaps permission to feel like a person again. He enters the office today not sure he can change, but certain he cannot go on as he is.
